messages.author: 618a80b31a9240ad
messages.subject: Why is Stan complaining here?
parts:
Dear users group (and beloved developers),

In the course of working on a stochastic SIR epidemiological model I've encountered some strange Stan behavior.

I've been able to isolate the problems with this a silly model which I would have expected Stan to have an easy time with:

parameters{
  vector[100] dw;
}
transformed parameters{
  real y;
  y = 1;
  for (n in 1:100){
    y = fmax(y + dw[n]*sqrt(y),0) ;
  }
}
model {
  dw ~normal(0,1);
}

When I run this with RStan 
sm <- stan_model(file="test_model.stan",verbose=FALSE)
system.time(sampling_results <- sampling(sm,iter=2000, chains=4,control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99)))


I get some:
The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times after warmup on chain 4
                                                         count
  Gradient evaluated at the initial value is not finite.    41
Rejecting initial value:                                    41
  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value.        41

and:
Warning messages:
1: There were 4000 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.99 may help. 
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems


and if I make that loop to be 200-long (with appropriately long dw) I even get:
[299] "  Gradient evaluated at the initial value is not finite."                                             
[300] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."                                                 
[301] "Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts. "                                           
[302] " Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."


Since there isn't any information in the model on observed an y value, it seems to me that the calculation of y should have no effect on the samplings of the dw parameters.

So why is Stan having a hard time?

p.s.:

Note, if I change the model block to:
model { 
   dw ~normal(0,1); 
   50 ~ normal(y,100); 
}
I still get thousands of divergent transitions 

However, if I make it:

model { 
   dw ~normal(0,1); 
   50 ~ normal(y,1); 
}

I still get things like:
  Gradient evaluated at the initial value is not finite.    37

But significantly fewer divergent transitions:
1: There were 169 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.99 may help. 


I find this strange as well. Why is it easier for stan to fit a tighter constraint?

(I am using rstan 2.10.0 on R 3.3.0 on linux)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why is Stan complaining here?
parts:
Without the transformed parameters block, this will obviously
be fine. What's happening is that y must be getting into a
bad state at some point, then trying to pass bad derivatives
back to the dw.

You want to print the values of y as they get
created and see where things go bad (and perhaps understand
y).

I don't know anything about these models or why you're
computing a y value you don't use (though I assume this is
just a trimmed down example).

Are you sure you don't want to constrain dw > 0?

It may be an underlying problem with how derivatives are
propagated (or not) through fmax. It's not continuously
differentiable, so we don't usually recommend using it
with parameters.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks for the quick reply.
y does not go berserk. I tried printing it out at the end of the loop and it stays well within the [0 4000] range.
In fact when I added:
  if (is_nan(y))
    print("y is NAN");
  if (is_inf(y))
    print("y is INF");
  if (y>4000)
    print("y large:", y);
I got no print outs at all.

If I add to model block:
  if(target()< -5000){
    print("lp  =",target()," y=",y);

I get a handful (<10) of printouts, in all those cases y=0.

I am still wondering why y is passing derivatives to dw if it does not participate in any log-probability updates (it shouldn't, correct?).
I guess the answer to that part would be te same as the one in this discussion:
https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/275
However, in the current case, y is nicely behaved...

Regarding the story behind my question:

In my true full model, "y" takes the form of the S, I, and R trajectories of a Stochastic Differential Equations (SDE) SIR model, these represent population size which are observed at some points and must be positive...
dw is a Wiener variable which is normally distributed.

A description of this SDE model is in this paper.
The paper does not discuss parameter estimation though, which is what I am doing with stan.
Problems arise at small population sizes (which is when the fmax takes affect).

Regards,
-- Lavi

On Wednesday, July 13, 2016 at 4:19:55 PM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Without the transformed parameters block, this will obviously
be fine.  What's happening is that y must be getting into a
bad state at some point, then trying to pass bad derivatives
back to the dw.

You want to print the values of y as they get
created and see where things go bad (and perhaps understand
y).

I don't know anything about these models or why you're
computing a y value you don't use (though I assume this is
just a trimmed down example).

Are you sure you don't want to constrain dw > 0?

It may be an underlying problem with how derivatives are
propagated (or not) through fmax.  It's not continuously
differentiable, so we don't usually recommend using it
with parameters.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why is Stan complaining here?
parts:
Ah, it's the sqrt(y); it's derivative is

d/dy sqrt(y) = 0.5 / sqrt(y)

which is a divide by zero error at y = 0.
The more iterations of that loop you do, the more
likely it is that you'll hit that boundary.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why is Stan complaining here?
parts:
We've run across other examples like this recently in
fisheries population models, where there's a stepwise
approximation of what's really a diff eq with a measured
catch which can drive the population negative if it's
larger than the previously estimated size.

If you explain more about your problem, we might be able
to help at a deeper level.

Often you can get by with some kind of constraint on variables
or with turning something you think is concrete into a measured
variable.

In general, fmax() is bad news in a Stan program because
it breaks derivatives. That is, no information flows from
the output of fmax() back to the system in cases where you
return a constant 0 and it's discontinuous in cases where
you don't when you cross the threshold.

- Bob
